newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croats protest at Serb celebration in Vukovar.
newsitem.headline: Croats protest at Serb celebration in Vukovar.

text.p: Croatia has urged the United Nations mission in the country's last Serb-held enclave to prevent Serbs there from celebrating their capture of the town of Vukovar in battle five years ago.

The U.N.'s transitional administration for Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), overseeing the region's return to Croatian rule, has already refused a request by Croat refugees from Vukovar to visit to the town on November 18, citing security reasons.

"I appeal to you on behalf of the entire Croatian public not to allow that songs and sounds of trumpets are heard in Vukovar on November 18," said Ivica Kostovic, a senior Croatian government official, in a letter sent to UNTAES on Sunday.

Vukovar, the largest city in Eastern Slavonia, was reduced to rubble in 1991 during a three-month siege by federal Yugoslav troops and minority Serbs opposed to Croatia's drive for independence from communist Yugoslavia.
Thousands of Croat families and fighters fled the town before the final Serb conquest on November 18.
Vukovar, which had a mixed ethnic population before the war, became a rallying cry for the Zagreb government.
Croatia recaptured all other Serb enclaves in two swift offensives in May and August last year.
Serb authorities in Eastern Slavonia announced earlier this week they would proclaim November 18 a public holiday to mark the fifth anniversary of the "liberation" of Vukovar.
The decision raised tensions in Croatia, where up to 100,000 refugees from Eastern Slavonia are keen to return to their homes.

"We think it's supreme cynicism on the part of local Serbs, and even the UNTAES, to celebrate the death of thousands of people who defended their town," said a protest from a refugee group from nearby, Croat-held, Vinkovci.

"On that same day in all other parts of the country, only sobbing and weeping will be heard," Kostovic said, warning that if the celebration went ahead it could harm the process of the reintegration of Eastern Slavonia into Croatia.

"Who will then be able to persuade our people, who saw the ruins of their homes for the last time on that very day, to go back and live peacefully with (the Serbs) who merrily celebrate the same day," he said.
The U.N. Security Council has extended the UNTAES mandate in the region until July 15 and analysts believe it could be ultimately extended for another six months, in full or reduced form.
